title: Is It Worth Your Budget? AI Training for Teachers
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd's budget-focused review argues that the market for teacher AI professional development has flipped in two years: major technology companies and professional organizations now give away full courses with certificates, while consultants still quote districts five figures for an in-service day. The piece rates nine categories of options on a five-star scale, from the Google and ISTE+ASCD micro-trainings and Code.org AI 101 to the ISTE Deep Dive, the NEA policy hub, vendor certifications such as MagicSchool, and paid university courses whose real value is state credit hours. Its central distinction is between AI literacy and product training, warning that a staff certified on one platform cannot evaluate the next tool. The review also surfaces an overlooked compliance issue, noting that AI detectors may send student work to third parties in ways that raise FERPA concerns. It closes with 'district math' (spend the saved money on release time for practice) and a two-month sequence that moves from foundations to policy, implementation artifacts, and rebuilding a single assignment, which the author calls the only step that changes anything.
points: A teacher can build real AI fluency this year for zero dollars, and a district can train a whole staff for close to it, because free courses now cover the ground consultants charge five figures for.
Vendor certification is product training rather than AI literacy; staff who complete it know one platform but not how to evaluate the next one, which is the durable skill.

The NEA hub flags that running student work through AI detectors may involve outside third parties and potential FERPA violations, making detector adoption a compliance question and not only a pedagogy question.

Most AI PD leaves buildings with enthusiasm and no governance, so the review prizes implementation artifacts such as use agreements, parent letters, and a script for talking with a student suspected of misusing AI.
The recommended sequence ends with rebuilding one assignment, and the review insists this practice step is the one everyone skips and the only one that changes classroom practice.
quotes: The result is that every major technology company and professional organization in education is now giving this away. Not a trial. Not a lead magnet. Full courses with certificates and, in some cases, graduate credit. Meanwhile consultants are quoting districts five figures for an AI in-service day.

Pro tip for leaders: If you are planning an AI in-service day, the facilitator guide here is free and covers the ground a consultant would charge for. Start there and spend your budget on release time instead.

This is the step nobody sells. You finish the Google training energized, walk into your classroom, and realize you still have to write a policy, explain it to families, and figure out what to say to the kid who obviously used ChatGPT.
Using a program to detect AI usage may require student work to be processed through an outside third party, which may be a FERPA violation.

This is product training, not AI literacy, and the two get conflated constantly. A staff that completes a vendor certification knows one platform. It does not know how to evaluate the next one, which is the durable skill.
Spend the difference on the thing money actually solves: paid time for teachers to sit down and use it. Training without practice time produces staff who have watched a video.

Artifacts, one hour. Before you teach anything, you need a policy, a family communication, and a plan for misuse. Adapt them from the TDI Hub or write your own, but do not skip this. Teachers who improvise the policy end up enforcing it inconsistently.
